summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

primary_citations.citation_text: New Mexico - NMSA 1978 Chapter 32A, Article 4 (Abuse and Neglect Act: 32A-4-3 duty to report, 32A-4-18 custody hearings, 32A-4-19 adjudicatory hearings), CYFD-published Children's Code compilation (2023 text; 32A-4-3 amended 2025 by SB 42)

New Mexico Statutes Chapter 27 - Public Assistance (public assistance and Medicaid programs; CYFD's child-welfare authority is not in this chapter — it is the Children, Youth and Families Department Act, NMSA 1978 § 9-2A-7(D), and the Children's Code, NMSA 1978 § 32A-1-1, per 8.10.3.3 NMAC)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers who failed to investigate abuse referrals and closed a foster child's case before he was starved and beaten to death were not entitled to qualified immunity, because the special relationship with a child in state custody and his right to reasonable safety were clearly established.
key_cases.relevance: Dismissing a foster child's case without investigating the referrals is precisely the screen-out failure this node covers, and here it defeated qualified immunity.
key_cases.quote: plaintiffs sufficiently pled facts, when taken as true, that show Booker and Peagler plausibly violated Chandler's substantive due process right to be reasonably safe while in foster care

key_cases.case_name: Yvonne L. v. New Mexico Department of Human Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that children in New Mexico state custody had a clearly established Fourteenth Amendment right to reasonable safety measured by the Youngberg professional judgment standard and reversed qualified immunity on that claim, while affirming that 42 U.S.C. Section 671(a)(10) of the AACWA is too vague and amorphous to be enforced under Section 1983.
key_cases.relevance: The court's professional-judgment standard reaches decisions not to screen or separate dangerous residents, the institutional analogue of a bad screening decision.
key_cases.quote: while it does not require actual knowledge the children will be harmed, it implies abdication of the duty to act professionally in making the placements

state_agency.name: New Mexico Children, Youth and Families Department

investigation_requirements: A local law enforcement officer trained in the investigation of child abuse and neglect is responsible for investigating reports of alleged child abuse or neglect at schools, daycare facilities or child care facilities (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(C))

If the child alleged to be abused or neglected is in the care or control of CYFD, or in a facility administratively connected to CYFD, the report must be investigated by a local law enforcement officer trained in the investigation of child abuse and neglect (NMSA 1978 § 32A-4-3(D))

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (one supervisor-approved extension of up to 30 additional days)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Statewide Central Intake accepts the report
